newsitem.title: UK: Buy Spain or Portugal bonds if Italy spooks.
newsitem.headline: Buy Spain or Portugal bonds if Italy spooks.

text.p: Bond market investors looking to cash in on the high yield rally in Europe could find richer rewards and lower risk on the Iberian peninsula than in Italy, analysts said on Thursday.

Fiscal belt-tightening and political credibility in Italy, Spain and Portugal will remain the critical issues in 1997 as each country struggles to squeeze budgets tight enough to qualify for planned European monetary union.
Spain and Portugal currently appear on track to meet their slimming targets and should be rewarded by more narrowing of yield spreads over German Bunds, analysts said.
Italy will follow suit but could prove the laggard of the group, they said.
"Portugal and Spain are the safer bets at the moment," said Adrian Schmidt, economist at Chase in London.
"I would put their chances for early entry (into EMU) as probable rather than possible. And Italy is only possible."

The stability pact for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) agreed to in Dublin last week brought the single currency a big step closer, allowing the convergence of high-yielding debt on Bunds to continue, analysts said.

Spreads on 10-year bond yields between Germany and both Spain and Portugal could narrow to 75 basis points (0.75 percentage point) in 1997 from around 115 currently, said Jose Luis Alzola, southern Europe economist at Salomon Brothers in London.

Italy may narrow the gap to 150 basis points from around 172 now but the move could take longer because of significant concern about the country's ability to bring its fiscal situation under control, he said.

"The economic fundamentals are improving more slowly and they have the added political risk," Alzola said. "There is real possibility of market disappointment. The market is attaching too much to the chances of Italy being in EMU from the beginning."

But if the government ultimately forces parliament to swallow a politically unappetising supplementary budget in 1997 and looks ripe for early EMU entry, Italian bonds could rally sharply and outperform other markets, said Juli Collins-Thompson, economist at Yamaichi in London.

She predicts the Italian spread over Bunds could reach the same level as Spain and Portugal by the end of next year. "We're very positive on the Italian front," Collins-Thompson said, highlighting the positive impact lower interest rates will have on the country's fiscal situation.
"There is the commitment there and they have ability to do it but they've got a division in politics in the lower chamber of parliament that they have to contend with," she said.

A potential spoiler amid the enthusiam for all three countries would be a postponement of EMU if France suffered further social unrest or the German government had a hard time selling EMU to a sceptical public, analysts said.
However, Italy, Spain and Portugal have demonstrated firm commitment to fiscal reform and even without EMU would not consider a change in course, they said.
"Spreads would widen, but they wouldn't be anywhere near the 400-500 level we had in early 1995," Alzola said.

A further risk for Spain and Portugal is the potential of being lumped into a "southern bloc" with Italy and kept out of the single currency because of Italy's failure to meet the Maastricht criteria, Chase's Schmidt said.
"That is the only question with Spain and Portugal. There is a perception politically that you can't have them in EMU without Italy," Schmidt said.
